text: — Oh! Bay Ganyo, Christ is risen! Were you at the palace for the Easter feast?

— Me, you mean? Why, if I don’t do it, who will? — replies Bay Ganyo to me, and, twirling his left mustache, gives me a sly wink, that is: “As long as there are fools in the world, your Uncle Ganyo won’t let a profit slip by.”
— So, how did it go? Was it fun?

— Well, who’s looking cheerful? There was profit in it, and plenty of it! I got myself cut up like... what’s-his-name... You know, on Passion Sunday I fasted, fasted, stuffed myself with that cursed bean stew, and on top of that army rations too; I was hungry as a wolf. On Saturday I didn’t put a crumb in my mouth. Then they went and set the Easter meal for two in the morning... While I was standing in church, it felt as if three hundred leeches were sucking at my belly. I spat and spat, and there wasn’t a drop of spit left. I’d try to light up — no use, it just tasted bitter in my mouth... They said, “Christ is risen” — it was twelve o’clock; how are you supposed to wait till two! I told my family to go and break the fast on their own, and I went into the “Red Crab.” There, my brother, it was full of people like me — top hats, epaulettes, orders. And they too were waiting for two o’clock to strike. I sat down at a long table and saw a few bachelors breaking the fast. They’d laid out that table of mine with all sorts of breakfast things, roast pig, and Varna wine on top of it — enough to make your stomach drip. Just looking at the piglet’s skin made my head spin. Well then, I should have asked those bachelors: “What are you eating there, eh? A pig? Bravo! Come on... what’s-his-name... a little bit with the skin...” — and the people would have given me some. But no. I’ve been shy since I was little... (Do pass me your tobacco case; you smoke good tobacco, Ivanov’s is no good at all, it smells like makhorka...) Those bachelors were smacking their lips, and I was sick of watching them, so I turned my eyes away. I thought I’d spit, but where was there any saliva! My insides were glued together. I thought of ordering a beer, but I felt sick. Was that what I’d been starving for, for two whole days... I turned away so as not to look at them, and they, as if on purpose, the devil take them, just kept chewing and praising the pig. I felt like getting up and snatching that cursed pig right out of their mouths... If only I could bend over and press my stomach a bit like that — hunger wouldn’t be so noticeable, but I can’t bend over. My frock coat is too tight; it’ll split open across the back. Ah, let the devil take it! And the collar was starched so stiff that it scraped my neck like a saw... My eyes went dark. I left the Crab and headed for the palace. You can’t go in early. I have a gendarme friend there, a good friend too, and if you ask me, he’s sort of a relative as well, but he never quite comes through. And even if you do go in early, it’s still no use — they won’t set the table for you right away. I wandered around the gates, wandered and wandered, and my legs started to ache. Then at last, drrr... one carriage, and a little later drrr... another carriage. They went into the palace, thank God! I twirled my moustache, coughed, and went after them. I went inside and saw the gendarmes, the escort, already lined up. A shaved-headed boy rushed up to take my coat off, and I muttered at him: “Excuse me, sir, mind your own business,” and I didn’t let him take it off. He got embarrassed and went to undress others. How could I let him take my coat off, brother? The sleeves of my coat, that is, not the sleeves, but the lining inside, were torn to pieces like... what’s-his-name. Anyway. I went upstairs, but before going up I cast an eye into the lower rooms — the tables were laid out, everything spotless. A crowd gathered. We waited a little here too, and then the prince and princess came out. This time they were, in a Christian way, truly host and hostess. They handed each of us an egg...
— Did you kiss a hand again?

— Well, hell’s bells... Why, for a feast like that I’d have kissed a hundred hands. Anyway. That ordeal too passed, for when we tumbled, my brother, down the stairs... Believe it or not, I was leaping three steps at a time; I was about to smash into the mirror, but I didn’t let anyone get ahead of me. I grabbed the caviar, and when I dug in with the spoon, if there was less than half a kilo of it — may it be a sin on my soul. That fish mayonnaise of yours, those little appetizers of mine, I don’t even know their names, for when those mouths of mine opened wide... Never mind!... I ate, I ate, I stuffed myself... and even now I wonder how my stomach didn’t burst. And the drinking... When I left, how I left — cut me open, I don’t remember... Uff!... My head still hurts from that damned champagne... And that’s not all — when I went and stuffed my pockets with pastries, and they were soft too, the devil take them, and they got all squashed in my pocket... Well, goodbye then.
